sentences.text: Buitreraptor possessed a slender, flat, and extremely elongated snout that was 25% longer than its femur.
This snout contained narrow, grooved, strongly recurved, and flattened teeth that lacked meat-tearing serrations.
The dinosaur had long forelimbs ending in very long and thin three-fingered hands where the digits were proportionally shorter and essentially equal in length.
The genus name Buitreraptor means "vulture raider," combining the Spanish word for vulture and the Latin word for seizer.
Fossils were found at the La Buitrera site, which translates to "vulture roost."
The dinosaur Buitreraptor was first described in 2005, with Buitreraptor gonzalezorum as its type species, and the work was published in the journal Nature.
Four specimens were discovered in 2004 in Patagonia, Argentina, during an excavation led by Sebastián Apesteguia and Peter Makovicky.
The specific name gonzalezorum honors the González brothers, Fabian and Jorge, who performed much of the excavation and preparation work.
Scientists concluded that Buitreraptor hunted small animals like lizards and mammals rather than large prey.
Buitreraptor likely swallowed prey whole because its teeth lacked serrations and functioned only to hold food.
Although no feathers have been found on Buitreraptor fossils, it is likely the dinosaur was feathered based on evidence from its close relatives.
Unenlagiines, including Buitreraptor, were better adapted for running and pursuit predation than the stockier Laurasian dromaeosaurids.
Buitreraptor was assigned to the family Dromaeosauridae in 2005.
Buitreraptor lived during the Early Cretaceous (Albian stage) in Argentina within the Candeleros Formation.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range for Buitreraptor as the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
